content.title: About
content.content: Beans are dried seeds of legume plants, obtained after thorough drying. They contain no added fat and are an excellent source of plant protein, complex carbohydrates, and dietary fiber. Beans are eaten boiled, stewed, and are also used to make flour, purees, and plant‑based meat alternatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans belong to the legume family and include varieties such as kidney beans, peas, chickpeas, and soybeans.
Dried beans can be stored for up to a year in a cool, dry place.
Beans have been used in cuisine since ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilizations.
Beans are rich in antioxidants, including flavonoids and phenolic compounds.
In many cultures beans are a symbol of abundance and prosperity.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beans provide 20–25 % protein, making them a valuable plant‑based protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Their complex carbs are digested slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and benefits gut health.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Beans contain iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, essential for normal body functions.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes beans suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting helps mitigate this.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Some beans (e.g., red kidney beans) contain toxins that are destroyed only by proper cooking.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas due to oligosaccharides; gradual introduction reduces the effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beans are boiled until tender and used in soups, stews, salads, or as a puree. They can be ground into gluten‑free flour for baking or added to smoothies for a protein boost. Soaking before cooking speeds up the process and lowers phytic acid content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, move them to the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth and nutrient loss.

content.title: About
content.content: Cabbage with ham hocks is a classic Russian dish consisting of stewed or boiled cabbage combined with pieces of ham hock (pork shank). The dish offers a rich aroma, balancing the natural sweetness of cabbage with the smoky flavor of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: It is traditionally prepared in colder months because it is hearty and warming.
The ham hock is usually browned first, then simmered with the cabbage to become tender and flavorful.
Soviet-era cookbooks often suggested adding tomato paste or dried mushrooms for extra depth.
Cabbage with ham hocks is commonly served alongside mashed potatoes or boiled potatoes.
Cooking in earthenware pots is traditional, as it preserves aroma and gives a deeper taste.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cabbage provides a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from cabbage aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Protein from ham hock
items.content: The ham hock supplies complete animal protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The dish offers potassium, magnesium, and iron, important for heart function and blood formation.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Cabbage with ham hocks fits well into moderately low‑carb eating patterns.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham hocks are often cured; people with hypertension should watch their salt intake.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Ham hocks can be fatty, so those monitoring fat consumption should eat the dish in moderation.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to pork should avoid this dish.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Pork must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of food‑borne illnesses.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, often directly from the earthenware pot. It can be enjoyed on its own or paired with mashed potatoes, boiled potatoes, or buckwheat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat thoroughly to a rolling boil before serving to ensure safety.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken curry with rice is an Indian-inspired dish where bite‑size pieces of chicken breast are simmered in a fragrant curry sauce made with coconut milk, tomatoes and spices, and served over fluffy rice. The dish balances spicy, slightly sweet flavors with a creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Curry is not a single recipe but a blend of spices that varies by region and personal taste.
Traditional Indian curry commonly uses turmeric, coriander, cumin, ginger and garlic, giving it a bright golden hue.
Coconut milk, often added to curry, mellows the heat of the spices and creates a richer sauce.
The dish is popular worldwide and has many variations, including Thai, Japanese and Caribbean styles.
Serving curry with rice provides a balanced intake of carbohydrates and protein, making it a hearty, nutritious meal.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains beneficial spices
items.content: Turmeric and ginger have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Turmeric stimulates bile production, while ginger eases digestive discomfort.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbohydrates that release glucose slowly, helping maintain energy levels.

items.title: Allergy to chicken or spices
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or specific spices such as coriander.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared curry sauces often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Watch coconut milk intake
items.content: Coconut milk is high in saturated fat; those watching cholesterol levels should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Chicken must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot curry over a portion of boiled or steamed rice. Garnish with fresh cilantro, a squeeze of lime, or a dollop of yogurt for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat until boiling to ensure any bacteria are destroyed.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken, meatless (NFS) is a plant‑based chicken fillet alternative made from soy protein, wheat gluten and natural flavorings. It mimics the taste and texture of real chicken and is intended for vegetarians and those reducing meat consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS (Not From Species) indicates the product contains no animal‑derived ingredients.
The fibrous texture is achieved through extrusion technology that replicates chicken muscle fibers.
The product is often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron to offset potential deficiencies in vegetarian diets.
It can be used in the same dishes as real chicken – salads, soups, stir‑fries, baked or grilled.
Production requires less water and land compared with conventional chicken farming.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A serving provides about 15–20 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Unlike real chicken, the substitute contains mainly polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Fortified iron helps prevent deficiency, especially in plant‑based diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Added B12 and B6 support normal nervous system function.

items.title: Environmental benefit
items.content: Manufacturing uses fewer resources, reducing the overall carbon footprint.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: The product contains soy protein, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat gluten is present, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are seasoned; consumers watching salt intake should check the label.

items.title: Processing additives
items.content: Thermal processing may introduce small amounts of additives and flavor enhancers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Meatless chicken can be pan‑fried, baked, steamed, or added to stews. Before cooking, rinse the pieces in cold water and pat dry. The product absorbs marinades and sauces well, allowing familiar flavor profiles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. Once opened, use within 5–7 days or refrigerate at 0–4 °C. Discard if you notice mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: The Italian sausage sandwich on white bread is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a slice of toasted white bread and a flavorful Italian sausage, usually pork‑based and seasoned with fennel, garlic, and spices. It is often served with mustard, mayo or marinara sauce, along with cheese slices and fresh vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Italian sausage (salami) originated in Southern Italy in the 19th century and quickly became a street‑food staple.
White bread became mass‑produced in the United States after industrial baking technologies emerged in the early 20th century.
The combination of spicy sausage and soft bread creates a texture contrast prized by sandwich lovers worldwide.
In some regions the sandwich is topped with fried onions and sweet peppers for a hint of sweetness.
Athletes often choose this sandwich as a quick meal because it provides protein and carbohydrates for rapid energy.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Italian sausage provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle repair and metabolic function.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Pork in the sausage is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and aids in red blood cell formation.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: White bread supplies fast‑acting carbohydrates that give an immediate energy boost, useful before workouts or during a busy day.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Seasonings like fennel and garlic contain antioxidants that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Italian sausage is often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure and strain the cardiovascular system.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The sausage contains saturated fats, which may increase cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to garlic, fennel, or other spices used in the sausage.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making the sandwich unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich hot, lightly toasted in a grill or toaster. Add a slice of cheese, lettuce, tomato, or pickles for freshness. Serve with fries, coleslaw, or a light dipping sauce of your choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep the sausage in its original packaging at 0 °C–4 °C. Bread should be kept in a dry place to prevent it from becoming stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard flavored gluten‑free pretzels are crunchy snack sticks made from gluten‑free flour and seasoned with natural flavorings such as cheese, onion, or paprika. They are suitable for people with gluten intolerance and anyone looking for a tasty, light bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels originated in Germany, where they are called "Brezel".
The hard texture is achieved by double‑baking and using gluten‑free flours like rice, corn, or buckwheat.
Flavorings are often derived from natural extracts, without artificial colors.
Gluten‑free pretzels gained popularity in the US after the rise of celiac disease awareness.
The traditional knot shape symbolizes crossed arms in prayer.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Most varieties contain no added sugar, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Gluten‑free flour provides slow‑release energy, helping to keep you full longer.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber from rice or buckwheat flour supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Some recipes are fortified with B1, B2, and B6 to aid metabolism.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Completely safe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: May contain soy sauce, dairy powder, or nut‑based flavorings that can trigger allergies.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Savory versions can have up to 400 mg of sodium per 30 g, which should be considered for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite being gluten‑free, pretzels are still calorie‑dense due to oil and starch.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels can be enjoyed straight from the bag, added to salads, soups, or used as a crunchy topping for cheese dishes. They are convenient for on‑the‑go snacking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain crispness and prevent staling.
